Emptiness
EMP-tee-nes
n.
From empty + -ness; empty from Old English æmtig (leisure, vacancy). Renders the Hebrew hebel, “vapor, breath, vanity” (Ecclesiastes’ great keyword), and the Greek kenosis-family of words, “an emptying.”

Biblical Definition

Emptiness in Scripture is a category that runs in two directions, the diagnostic and the doctrinal—and the most surprising of the two is the doctrinal one. Diagnostically, the Bible names the emptiness of created things apart from God as the deep verdict of the Preacher of Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. The Hebrew hebel means literally vapor, breath—the visible exhalation on a winter morning, present for a moment and then gone. The Preacher applies this verdict to wealth, pleasure, wisdom, work, fame, even life itself when considered apart from God: each is a vapor, briefly substantial, ultimately empty. The diagnostic emptiness is therefore the great Old Testament wisdom verdict on the creature’s self-sufficient pursuit of meaning apart from its Creator: every pursuit, however richly stocked, ends in the same vapor. Doctrinally, however, the most surprising biblical emptiness is the kenosis of the Son of God in the incarnation. Philippians 2:7: Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation (literally, emptied himself, heauton ekenosen), and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men. The Son did not cease to be God; the kenosis is not the emptying of the divine nature but the laying-aside of the independent use of divine prerogatives, the assumption of true humanity, the willingness to live the divine-human life under the conditions of the form of a servant, all the way to the death of the cross. The believer’s emptiness is a third register, derivative of the second. The saint, having seen the Son’s self-emptying, learns to empty himself of self-righteousness, self-trust, and self-aggrandizement, and to receive the fulness that the empty Christ has secured for the empty sinner. The Beatitude of the poor in spirit is this emptiness preceding fulness; the doctrine of justification by faith alone rests on the empty hand of faith that contributes nothing; the Christian life is the long discipline of being emptied of self that the soul may be more thoroughly filled with the fulness of Christ. The three emptinesses therefore stand in their proper relation: the diagnostic emptiness of every creature pursuit apart from God; the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son for our salvation; and the experiential emptying of the saint that conforms him, in measure, to the pattern of his Lord and prepares him to receive His fulness.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines EMPTINESS as the state of being empty; want of contents; vacuity; void space; figuratively, want of substance or solidity; want of value; in scripture, the vanity of created things apart from God (Ecclesiastes) and the self-emptying of Christ in the incarnation (Phil 2:7).

EMPTINESS, n. — 1. A state of being empty; destitution of contents; vacuity; void space. 2. Want of substance or solidity; vanity; unsatisfactoriness. 3. Want of intellect or knowledge; vacuity of head; want of intelligence. 4. In scripture, the vanity (Heb. hebel, vapor) of created things considered apart from God, as in Ecclesiastes; and the kenosis of the Son in the incarnation (Phil 2:7).

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 1:2 — "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity."

Philippians 2:6-7 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men."

Matthew 5:3 — "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Jeremiah 2:5 — "Thus saith the LORD, What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?"

Modern Corruption

Emptiness is corrupted, on the diagnostic side, by the affluent-distraction culture that has masked the Ecclesiastes verdict so successfully that whole lifetimes of meaningful pursuit can be lived without the soul ever facing it—and on the doctrinal side by the kenotic-Christology error that reads Phil 2:7 as Christ’s actual emptying of His divine attributes rather than the laying-aside of their independent use.

expand to see more

The affluent-distraction culture of the late-modern West has masked the Ecclesiastes verdict so successfully that whole lifetimes of meaningful-looking pursuit can be lived without the soul ever facing it. The Preacher’s diagnosis—that wealth, pleasure, wisdom, work, fame, and life itself considered apart from God are vapor—is fenced off from the contemporary believer’s daily experience by an endless supply of distractions, achievements, comforts, and stimulations that prevent the deep emptiness from being felt. The cure is partly providential (the providences that strip the masks: bereavement, failure, illness, the encounter with one’s mortality), partly disciplined (the deliberate silence, the fast, the prayer that lets the emptiness rise), and partly evangelistic (the gospel preached so that the emptiness, once felt, has the answer of the Christ who Himself was emptied to fill the empty). Recover the diagnostic emptiness, and the gospel recovers its addressees: the soul that has not faced its emptiness cannot receive the fulness Christ supplies.

The doctrinal corruption of the kenosis is the late-19th and 20th-century kenotic-Christology error, which reads Phil 2:7 as Christ’s actual emptying of His divine attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) during the incarnation, so that the Christ of the Gospels is divinity-minus rather than divinity-veiled. The historic Reformed and Lutheran tradition has rejected this reading on several grounds: it contradicts the Chalcedonian definition (the two natures unconfused and unchanged); it leaves the church with a Christ who, during His earthly life, was not the One in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwelt bodily (against Col 1:19; 2:9); and it makes the Son’s ongoing upholding of all things by the word of His power (Heb 1:3) impossible during the incarnation. The orthodox reading holds Phil 2:7 as the laying-aside of the independent use of divine prerogatives and the assumption of true humanity, not the laying-aside of deity itself. Recover both ends. The diagnostic emptiness opens the soul; the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son provides the answer; the believer’s emptiness empties him of self that he may be filled with the fulness of the Christ whose own self-emptying in the incarnation was, all the way through, the act of the Son who remained what He always was—true God and now also true man, full of grace and truth.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hebel (vapor, breath, vanity—Ecclesiastes’ great word) and rīq (emptiness, vanity); Greek kenōsis-family from kenoō (to empty—Phil 2:7)—three biblical emptinesses: the diagnostic vapor of creature pursuit, the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son, and the experiential emptying of the saint.
